children.text: A cluster of skyscrapers, SM Megamall, Robinsons Galleria and The Podium line up east of EDSA in Metro Manila's second business district. See recent history at the EDSA Shrine, shop and dine in the malls, then watch the city lights from a hotel rooftop bar on a half-day to one-day urban route.

Ortigas Center is a business district east of EDSA, bounded by Ortigas Avenue to the north, Meralco Avenue to the east and Shaw Boulevard to the south. It covers only about 1 km² (just over 100 hectares), but it straddles the borders of three cities, Pasig, Mandaluyong and Quezon City, so a single district carries addresses from three different places. It is Metro Manila's second central business district after Makati, packed with corporate headquarters, banks, large malls and hotels. It is less a place for ticking off famous sights than a place to wander between air-conditioned malls and office towers and watch everyday city life in Manila.
The land was once the roughly 4,000-hectare Hacienda de Mandaloyon, owned by Augustinian friars. On
January 20, 1920
the order sold the estate to Frank W. Dudley and Don Francisco Ortigas, and on

Ortigas & Company was formally incorporated. The district's name comes from the Ortigas family. As the estate turned into a business, commercial and residential district, the Ortigas Center Association was founded in
, and it still oversees the district's development and management today. The murals and signs in Ortigas Park tell this story of development in pictures.
What changed the face of the district was the early
. Robinsons Galleria opened on
January 12, 1990
, SM Megamall on
and Shangri-La Plaza on
November 21, 1991
, and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) moved its headquarters here to Mandaluyong on
. The northern tip, where EDSA meets Ortigas Avenue, is where crowds gathered during the People Power Revolution in
February 1986

, and the EDSA Shrine built in thanks for it still stands there. Shopping malls, an international organization, corporate headquarters and a site of history all overlap within one district, and that is what gives Ortigas Center its character.

The district falls roughly into three zones. In the north, on the Quezon City side, are the EDSA Shrine and Robinsons Galleria; in the west, on the Mandaluyong side, are SM Megamall, The Podium, Shangri-La Plaza and the Asian Development Bank; and in the east, on the Pasig side, are high-rises such as the San Miguel headquarters and bank buildings. Even among Metro Manila's downtown areas, each has its own character.
BGC
is a planned new town built on a former military base, charming for its wide sidewalks and murals, while
Makati

offers museums and gardens along Ayala Avenue and the nightlife of the Poblacion lanes. Ortigas Center is humbler and more practical than both. The malls sit right next to EDSA and the MRT stations, so it is a good place to spend time indoors on rainy days or to escape the midday heat, and after dark you can watch the night view from a high-rise hotel's sky bar. It suits travelers who want to combine shopping, dining, city sightseeing and a site of modern history like the EDSA Shrine in half a day to a day.

The mood changes a lot depending on when you visit. On weekday afternoons the food courts and cafés fill with office workers at lunchtime (noon–1 p.m.), and EDSA and Ortigas Avenue are at their most congested at rush hour (5–8 p.m.). On weekends the office towers quiet down, while every mall fills with families and young people out for movies and shopping. As a traveler, the easiest flow is to see the EDSA Shrine and the park on a weekday morning or early afternoon, then move to the malls and a sky bar around sunset. Most of the sightseeing is indoors and involves short hops, so it is not much of a burden for children or parents either.
This large mall on the corner of EDSA and Julia Vargas Avenue opened on
. Buildings A, B and C connect to the Mega Fashion Hall, which opened on
January 28, 2014
and has an Olympic-size ice rink and an IMAX theater. The neighboring Mega Tower is a 50-storey,
office building. SM announced a redevelopment plan in
June 2024
and demolished part of Building A, so check before you go whether any area is closed for construction.
Opened on
January 12, 1990

, it was the first and flagship store of Robinsons Malls. The five-storey building holds around 400 shops and restaurants, and the Crowne Plaza and Holiday Inn hotels are attached to the same complex. It lies at the northern end of Ortigas Center, within easy walking distance of the EDSA Shrine and the MRT Ortigas station.
The shrine was built in gratitude for the
People Power Revolution and consecrated on
December 15, 1989
. Its architect was Francisco Mañosa, and in the middle of the plaza a bronze "Our Lady of Peace" statue about
tall stands with outstretched arms. It was designated an Important Cultural Property in
and received national shrine status from the bishops' conference on
January 25, 2025
. It is an open space that anyone can visit, and a good place to sense the history of democracy in modern Philippines.
This mall of roughly 50,000 m² opened in
August 2002

, and the vertical garden covering its façade stands out from afar. It has many cafés and restaurants and is a popular spot for meals, and ADB Avenue in front has a dedicated bike lane, which makes it a pleasant place to walk or cycle while looking up at the surrounding high-rises.
A large mall on the Mandaluyong side that opened on
November 21, 1991
, it connects directly to the MRT Shaw Boulevard station. It has about 300 shops and restaurants spread over many floors, a cinema on levels 6 and 7, and the Edsa Shangri-La hotel right next door.

A small urban park at the intersection of Ruby Road and Opal Road. There are shade trees and lawns among the high-rises, and murals and signs on the park walls show how the Ortigas family developed the district, starting from the days of the Hacienda de Mandaloyon. It is a nice spot to rest for a while as you move between malls.
Vu's Sky Bar & Lounge on the roof of the Marco Polo Ortigas Manila hotel is the best-known place to look down on Ortigas Center's night view. It opens Monday to Saturday from
5 p.m. to 1 a.m.
and is closed on Sundays; guests must be 18 or older, and the dress code is smart casual.
Estancia in the Capitol Commons complex, where Meralco Avenue meets Shaw Boulevard, is an open-air mall with shops and restaurants lining the street. Tiendesitas in Ortigas East, about
3 km
east of the center, is a market-cum-shopping area that opened in
and gathers crafts, antiques and food stalls. It belongs to the same Ortigas family of developments but lies outside the business district, so go there separately by car.

items.title: Taxi or Grab from Manila airport

children.text: From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) to Ortigas Center it is about
14 km
, and it takes
30 minutes to 1 hour 10 minutes
depending on traffic. It takes longer at rush hour.
Airport guidance puts the taxi meter fare to Ortigas Center at roughly
(tolls extra), and Grab is shown at about
. From
September 28, 2026
the base fare of app-based rides (TNVS) rose 20% depending on vehicle type and the airport taxi flag-down rose to ₱115, so check the fare in the app first.
Avoid private drivers touting for customers outside the arrivals hall; use the official taxi queue or the Grab pickup area.
MRT-3's Ortigas station sits in the middle of EDSA, about
7.9 km
from North Avenue station at the northern end. Shaw Boulevard station (directly connected to Shangri-La Plaza) is the very next stop.
The fare is about
depending on the number of stations, and the government announced a 50% fare discount on MRT-3 and LRT-2 from
March 23, 2026
. Check at the station counter whether it still applies.
This line carried an average of about 390,000 passengers a day in
, so it is very crowded at rush hour (7–9 a.m., 5–8 p.m.). Carry your bag in front of you and watch out for pickpockets.
The Carousel buses that run in the EDSA bus lane pass through Ortigas Center, and the Ortigas stop is the median stop next to the MRT Ortigas station.
The fare is about
for the first
4 km
and rises with distance after that. Cash is easiest, but Beep cards may also work, so check when you board.
Many jeepneys run between Ortigas Avenue and EDSA, and UV Express vans head toward Makati and Quezon City. From
September 28, 2026
the minimum fare rose to
for a regular jeepney and
for a modern jeepney.
Ask a local to confirm the route name, and tell the driver where you want to get off in advance.
From
BGC
, thanks to the BGC–Ortigas link road completed in
October 2021
, it takes about
12–30 minutes
by car (depending on traffic).
From Ayala in
Makati
it takes around
30 minutes to 1 hour
by taxi or Grab, and EDSA is heavily congested at rush hour.
The EDSA Shrine, Galleria, SM Megamall and Shangri-La Plaza all line EDSA, but they are
1–2 km
apart each, so mix in the MRT or a taxi to avoid the daytime heat.
Around Meralco Avenue some roads may be blocked or need a detour because of construction of the Metro Manila Subway's Ortigas station.
Metro Manila's dry season runs
December–May
, and
December–February
is the coolest part of it. The average daytime high in January is about
, the best time to walk around the district.
March–May
is hot and dry, and in April the average high climbs to about

, so spend the daytime in the malls and indoors and go out in the morning and around sunset. Because the district is built around malls, one advantage is that it is easy to plan indoor activities in any season.
During the
June–November
rainy season, sudden showers are frequent, and typhoons pass most often in
June–September

. In July and August it rains on nearly 19 days a month, and when a downpour hits, water collects on EDSA and the district's roads and traffic gets extremely bad. If rain is forecast, bring your plans forward and avoid the rush hour (5–8 p.m.). In
December
the malls are full of Christmas decorations and sales and the district is at its liveliest.

There are roughly three kinds of places to stay. The most convenient are the hotels inside the district, represented by the Crowne Plaza and Holiday Inn in the Robinsons Galleria complex, the Edsa Shangri-La and the Marco Polo Ortigas Manila. A 4–5 star room runs about
a night depending on the date. To save money, choose an economy hotel such as Go Hotels or Red Planet on the edge of the district (about

a night); many of these are within walking distance of an MRT station or a mall. Ortigas Center is a business district, so it is busy on weekday afternoons and quiet on weekend evenings, and hotel prices often drop on weekends.
Almost every kind of food is available inside the malls. A food-court meal costs about

, and The Podium, Shangri-La Plaza and SM Megamall have Japanese, Korean, Western food and cafés on every floor. Jollibee Tower, the headquarters of the Philippines' signature fast-food chain Jollibee, is also in this district, so Jollibee is easy to find anywhere. If you miss Korean food you can find Korean restaurants in malls such as The Podium, and there is also Cantonese cooking at the Marco Polo hotel and a range of Asian restaurants on the Mandaluyong side. For a more local restaurant district, take a taxi to nearby Kapitolyo in Pasig, where Filipino and Southeast Asian restaurants in converted houses, Italian places and cafés cluster along the lanes. Shops change often, so check on a map app whether a place is open before you go.

For brunch and bread, Wildflour Café + Bakery at The Podium has long been well known. If a drink and a night view are what you want, Vu's Sky Bar on the roof of the Marco Polo hotel has been counted as the district's signature sky bar since around
. Drinks and bar snacks cost more than at the mall restaurants, so go up around sunset and enjoy the view over a cocktail or two.
Malls usually open at 10 a.m. and close at 9–10 p.m. The hours that were cut during the energy emergency in
March 2026
returned to normal at most malls from late
June
, but this can differ by mall, so check before you visit.
Most malls have strong air conditioning. A thin jacket makes it less chilly indoors.
You pass a bag check and a metal detector at mall entrances. If you carry a large backpack or suitcase, check the luggage storage notice.
The EDSA Shrine is a religious site. Avoid revealing clothes and stay quiet during Mass. Mass times change, so check on the
official website
or with the shrine.
At Vu's Sky Bar, shorts, sandals and sleeveless tops may get you turned away. It is safest to reserve before you go.
Using Grab rather than a taxi lets you know the fare in advance. Waits are long at rush hour, so book with time to spare.
When it rains, the sidewalks in the district get slippery and some roads flood. Use the overpasses and indoor passages that connect the malls.
Lunchtime (noon–1 p.m.) brings long lines at food courts and popular restaurants. Eating a little earlier or later is more relaxed.
Malls take cards widely, but small stalls, taxis and jeepneys prefer cash. Carry plenty of small bills.
If you shop, bargaining is possible at the tiangge market in neighboring Greenhills, but compare prices at several places before buying high-value items such as pearls.
The area around the EDSA Shrine was the scene of large rallies, including the "Trillion Peso March" against corruption, from
September 2025
to
February 2026
. On rally days EDSA traffic is controlled and crowds gather, so avoid the shrine on those dates or check the news.
In the
July 2026

regular adjustment of travel advisories, Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs kept the Zamboanga Peninsula and the Sulu, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi island groups on its travel ban list, and Metro Manila is not included. Still, check the current advisory on the Ministry's overseas safety travel site before you leave.
Pickpocketing and phone snatching happen on the MRT, on jeepneys and on the sidewalks outside malls. Do not take your smartphone out on the road side, and carry your bag in front of you.
In heavy rain in the wet season, EDSA and the district's roads flood and taxis are hard to find. If a typhoon is forecast, cut back your outdoor plans.
SM Megamall may see construction under its redevelopment plan, and construction of the subway's Ortigas station is under way near Meralco Avenue. You may meet blocked roads, noise and detour signs.
The Metro Manila Subway is due to open in
, so it cannot be used on your trip. Even if guides mention reaching the district by subway, it is not yet available.
